what_this_milestone_is: The mission's product milestone: /organization/access derives and displays authoritative state, and the authorization paths underlying those claims are enforced. Presentation reflects authorization; presentation does not create authorization.

shipped_this_session.workstream: W-51 — IA-7, and the M2-17 composition the plan records but does not price
shipped_this_session.defect_display: user_roles is keyed on (user_id, org_id, role), so a membership is a SET. displayRoleForAdminPicker collapsed it and four places rendered the survivor as the whole answer: the roster row, the detail header, the Overview's Role field, and the search haystack — where a member holding {admin, regional_lead} was unfindable by 'regional lead'.
shipped_this_session.defect_counts: The Roles chapter counted members by the collapsed value and filtered its Users tab the same way, so a role that is never anyone's primary reported ZERO holders while the resolver was unioning its grants into live requests. Both now ask one predicate, so the count and the list cannot disagree.
shipped_this_session.defect_destructive: M2-17. The read collapses, the editor is seeded from the collapsed value, and PATCH /api/admin/users/[userId]/role replaces EVERY role row for the pair. Changing the one visible role of a principal holding {admin, regional_lead} deleted regional_lead, having never shown it. The one guard present made it worse: disabling the save while editRole === primary_role removed the harmless no-op and left only the submissions that reach the destructive path.
shipped_this_session.remedy: replacementIsNoOp asks the union, so a multi-role membership is correctly reported as a change; the loss is itemized by name; the save requires an explicit acknowledgement that resets on any change of principal or target; and the guard sits in front of the write in saveRole, not only on the button — a disabled attribute is a presentation fact, and this platform's rule is that presentation reflects authorization rather than creating it.
shipped_this_session.scope_limit_stated: This does NOT make the write additive. That is W-17, which needs an API that can add a role without removing the others. Until then the control says 'Replace with', because that is what it does. The card's claim that 'One role is supported per user today' described the picker, not the platform, and is gone.
shipped_this_session.why_not_deferred_to_W_17: The plan sequences IA-7 with W-17 because W-17 makes multi-role reachable. But multi-role memberships already exist — the plan's own census names one — so the display half is a present untruth and the destructive half is present data loss. Neither needs W-17 to be worth closing, and neither preempts its design.

shipped_this_session.workstream: Tier C — the eleven-fixture certification matrix
shipped_this_session.why_this_shape: The mission's acceptance form is that the UI, the route/API, and effective authorization AGREE — not that each behaves defensibly alone. Three passing per-layer suites can still describe a surface hidden in navigation and reachable by URL. Every fixture therefore derives all three answers and asserts the agreement itself, including as a set-cardinality check so a change that moves all four consumers together in the WRONG direction still has to move them together.
shipped_this_session.the_route_answer_is_the_route_s: requireUsersRolesManageAuth runs with its access-context dependency mocked at the module boundary. What is certified is the helper the Access routes actually call. That the mock is in effect is self-evidencing: the real resolver cannot return 200 without a database.
shipped_this_session.defect_found_in_own_work: The URL-reachability assertion was tautological on first writing — `reachable` and `offered` were the same expression, certifying nothing. Rewritten to compose the page's two refusals in the page's order from the exported predicates; that the page applies them in that order is proved separately by RL-36 against the real page source.
fixtures: capability permits but scope excludes the target
shipped_this_session.layer_separation_proved: F9 is admitted by capability and still bounded to one location; F1 holds the same capability bounded by nothing. The distinction is therefore real and not an artifact of every fixture being restricted.
shipped_this_session.negatives_asserted_directly: For every unset-profile fixture: scopeSummary must NOT return 'All locations', certainty is 'unset', the divergence reason is present, and allow-list rows are withheld. IA-3 as a test rather than a claim.

shipped_this_session.workstream: W14-F1 — the disclosure half, which was never the half that needed a decision
shipped_this_session.why_this_was_actionable: W-14 recorded the finding and declined to answer it because asserting that a roster read needs no capability is W-15's product call. That reasoning is correct and unchanged — and it was applied to the wrong half. The finding has two: WHO REACHES the route is a product question; WHAT IT DISCLOSES to whoever reaches it is not. Only the first needed an operator.
shipped_this_session.defect: GET /api/admin/users is admitted by portal eligibility alone and returned every org member's email address to everyone it admitted. The live consumer that made this matter is components/admin/opportunity/OperationalWorkAssigneeSelect.tsx, which needs to NAME a colleague in an assignee dropdown and derived that name from the local-part client-side — `label: row.email?.trim() || row.label` — so the full address crossed the wire in order to be rendered whole. Any staffer who could assign work could read the organisation's entire email list out of a <select>.
shipped_this_session.remedy: The label is computed at the route for every caller; the address is projected against canManageUsersAndRoles. No consumer loses a function — the picker shows the same names, the Access surface reads from the gated members route as before, and the legacy tables already handled email === null, which has always been in AdminUserRow's contract for an unreadable auth record.
shipped_this_session.admission_deliberately_unchanged: The declaration stays 'pending' rather than being quietly resolved, and its note is AMENDED rather than cleared. The gate is read from the bundle getAdminContextCached already resolved, so it costs no second auth pass — and it must NOT be re-derived from getAdminAccessContextCached, which does not require portalEligible and would widen who reaches the route while appearing to tighten it. Two tests assert that exact accident, one of them a caller who is portal-refused while holding the managing grant.
shipped_this_session.certification_shape: The agreement tests run the real handler and feed its real JSON to the real consumer's fetcher, then assert what the dropdown would put on screen. Three passing per-layer suites can still describe a route that withholds an address and a component that renders one from somewhere else.
shipped_this_session.non_vacuity: Proved by defeating the gate: the two disclosure assertions fail and the other thirteen do not.
shipped_this_session.still_open: The admission question. W14-F1 is NOT closed — its disclosure half is.

shipped_this_session.workstream: The backing-route record is discovered, not enumerated
shipped_this_session.defect_class: A sound check over an unsound subject. surfaceCapabilityDeclaration asserts that every route a chapter NAMES declares that chapter's capability, but backingRoutes is hand-authored — so a chapter calling a route nobody wrote down does not fail the join, it never enters it. This initiative has already been bitten by this shape (W-5, 'does the lock DISCOVER or ENUMERATE?').
shipped_this_session.measurement: The Users chapter issues six requests and declared three; the Roles chapter issues four and declared two. Six omissions.
shipped_this_session.why_nothing_was_broken: Every omitted route is correctly gated — users POST, users/[userId]/remove, rbac/roles, rbac/roles/[role_key], rbac/permissions and rbac/grants all declare settings.users_roles in W-14's table. Which is precisely why nothing said anything. A record that can only be audited by the person who wrote it is not a control.
shipped_this_session.remedy: The declaration is completed, and the new lock's subject is DISCOVERED from each chapter's own source, with dynamic segments normalised on both sides so `[userId]` and `${encodeURIComponent(id)}` compare as one path.
shipped_this_session.grain_decides_the_classification: capabilitiesDeclaredBy unions over a file's methods, and the divergence ratchet asserts a divergent route does NOT declare the capability. rbac/roles, rbac/grants and rbac/permissions read through requirePortalOrUsersRolesManageAuth, which admits portal-eligible principals lacking the grant — wider than the chapter's gate. They are still BACKING routes, because their files DO declare settings.users_roles; the wider read leg is recorded in W-14's table as W-13's portal.access question. Listing them as divergent would have failed the ratchet and stated something false.
shipped_this_session.non_vacuity: Removing rbac/permissions from the roles declaration makes the lock name that exact route and fail.

tier_D_environment.class: operator-owned, environmental — not a product decision
tier_D_environment.what: Browser certification of /organization/access cannot be run from this session.
evidence: This worktree has no dev-server metadata: `alloy-dev-start wt6-director-experience-dx5-5-continuation` returns 'unknown worktree metadata'. Only seven worktrees are registered and this is not one of them.

Slot 6 in the registry is assigned to a DIFFERENT worktree (wt6-search-platform-certification), so every slot-numbered command — alloy-dev-start 6, alloy-agent-login 6, alloy-agent-verify 6 — would target the wrong tree. This is the 'resolve worktrees by NAME, not slot number' hazard, live.
Slot 6's stored auth reports `missing`, so even the registered tree has no QA identity session.

web/.env.local.agent carries only public/anon values, by design — no service-role key. Every Access admin route calls createAdminClient(), so an unbrokered server would fail on exactly the routes under certification.
tier_D_environment.re_verified_session_3: Still true, checked rather than inherited. `alloy-dev-start wt6-director-experience-dx5-5-continuation` returns 'unknown worktree metadata'; the metadata directory holds seven entries and this worktree is not among them; slot 6 resolves to wt6-search-platform-certification (a different path, on branch agent/claude/6-search-platform-certification, auth 'missing'). Nothing about the blocker has changed and nothing was worked around.
tier_D_environment.what_would_unblock_it: Register this worktree with the dev toolkit (or re-point slot 6 at it) and run alloy-agent-login, after which alloy-agent-verify can produce route evidence for /organization/access.
tier_D_environment.not_worked_around: No dev server was started by another path. The governance forbids bare `next dev`, and privileged values are deliberately absent from the worktree; manufacturing a server here would have produced evidence from an environment the product does not run in.

findings_left_open.W49-F1: app/api/admin/send-password-reset/route.ts — the chapter renders 'Send password reset' to every holder of settings.users_roles; the route enforces ctx.role !== 'admin'. A grant-holder who is not org admin is shown the control and gets 403. Declaring it settings.users_roles would be a one-line WIDENING of who may trigger a password-reset email — W-15's sweep with a product decision behind it. Pinned in RL-36.
findings_left_open.W14-F1: HALF CLOSED (4612d4d2d). The disclosure half is done: GET no longer returns any member's address to a caller without settings.users_roles. The ADMISSION half stands open and unchanged — whether a roster read should require a capability at all is still W-15's product call, and the route's declaration remains 'pending' to say so. Do not read the amended note as a resolved finding.
